title: Best Juice for a Hangover: What Helps, What Hurts, What's Hype
excerpt: Which juice actually helps a hangover? An honest ranking of coconut water, tomato, orange, Korean pear, pickle, apple, cranberry and more, plus what to avoid and how much to drink.
metaDescription: The best juice for a hangover, ranked: coconut water, tomato, orange, Korean pear and more. What each one helps, what to avoid, and how much to drink.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** no juice cures a hangover, but some juices are more useful the morning after than others. The best choices are the ones that put back what a night of drinking actually takes out of you: fluid, some sodium and potassium, and a little easy sugar for energy. By that measure, **coconut water** and **low-sodium or regular tomato juice** are the most practical picks, **orange juice** is a decent option if your stomach is calm, and **Korean pear juice** is the only juice with a small human study behind it, though it only seemed to help when people drank it *before* drinking alcohol. Juices sold as "detox" or "cleanse" drinks don't do anything special for your liver, and very sugary or acidic juices can make a queasy stomach or heartburn worse.

**The quick rules:** Drink water or an electrolyte drink first, then add a modest glass of juice (about 6 to 8 ounces) if it sounds good. Dilute juice half-and-half with water if your stomach is unsettled. Pair it with some salty food, because most fruit juices are low in sodium. Skip grapefruit juice if you take prescription medicines. And keep expectations realistic: juice helps with the dried-out, low-energy part of a hangover, not the headache and fog that come from poor sleep and your body's reaction to alcohol.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover after a night out is miserable but gets better on its own within a day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or see blood (or something that looks like coffee grounds) in your vomit, you have severe stomach pain, you're barely urinating, or you feel confused, faint, or have a racing heart that won't settle. If someone can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin, call 911. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover, and no drink at home will fix them. If you have diabetes, kidney disease, or heart failure, talk to your doctor about which drinks are right for you, since juice sugar and potassium matter more for you.

## What a Juice Can and Can't Do for a Hangover

To pick the right juice, it helps to know what a hangover is made of. Researchers who study hangovers describe it as several problems happening at once:

- **Fluid and salt loss.** Alcohol blocks a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you urinate more than you drink. Vomiting and sweating add to the loss.
- **Low energy and shaky blood sugar.** Your liver is busy processing alcohol, which can interfere with how it releases sugar into the blood. Many people also skip dinner or eat little before bed.
- **Irritated stomach.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which is why nausea and heartburn are so common the next day.
- **Inflammation and alcohol by-products.** Your body breaks alcohol down into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, and drinking triggers an inflammatory response. Researchers think these are big drivers of the headache, aches, and "poisoned" feeling.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it breaks up sleep in the second half of the night.

A juice can genuinely help with the first two: it's fluid, it often carries potassium, and its natural sugar gives you quick energy. It does almost nothing for the last three. That's why the most honest way to rank juices is by how well they rehydrate and how kind they are to your stomach, not by which vitamins appear on the label.

## The Best Juices for a Hangover, Ranked

Here's a side-by-side look. Nutrition numbers are rough averages for an 8-ounce (240 ml) glass of plain, unsweetened juice and vary a lot by brand, so check the label on the one you buy.

| Juice | What it brings | Watch out for | Overall verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coconut water | Fluid, a lot of potassium, little sugar | Low in sodium; large amounts not for people with kidney disease | One of the best everyday picks |
| Tomato juice | Fluid, a lot of sodium and potassium, low sugar | Regular versions are very salty; acidic for heartburn | Great for salt loss, if your stomach tolerates it |
| Orange juice | Fluid, potassium, quick sugar, vitamin C | Acidic; easy to drink too much sugar | Good if your stomach is calm |
| Korean (Asian) pear juice | One small human study, before drinking | Sugar; untested as a next-day fix | Best as a pre-drinking habit, not a cure |
| Watermelon juice | Mostly water, some potassium | Little sodium; sugar adds up | Pleasant, hydrating, nothing magic |
| Pickle juice (brine) | A strong hit of sodium | Very salty; not for blood pressure or heart issues | A salty add-on, in small sips |
| Apple juice | Gentle, low acid, quick sugar | High in sugar, little else | Fine diluted if your stomach is sore |
| Cranberry juice | Fluid | Usually heavily sweetened; no "detox" effect | Not a standout |
| Grape juice | Quick sugar | One of the most sugary juices | Skip or dilute heavily |
| Grapefruit juice | Fluid, vitamin C | Interacts with many prescription medicines; acidic | Avoid if you take medication |
| Lemon water | Fluid, a little flavor | No real detox effect | Fine if it gets you drinking water |

The sections below explain each one and when it makes sense.

## Coconut Water: The Most Balanced Everyday Choice

Coconut water is naturally lower in sugar than most fruit juices and rich in potassium, which is why it's marketed as "nature's sports drink." It's easy on the stomach, mild in flavor, and most people can drink a full glass even when they feel rough.

Its weakness is sodium. Sodium is the main electrolyte you lose through urine, sweat, and vomiting, and it's the one that helps your body actually hold on to the water you drink. Most coconut water has far less sodium than an oral rehydration drink. Small studies comparing coconut water with sports drinks for rehydration after exercise have generally found it works about as well as plain water or a sports drink, but people sometimes find it harder to drink in large amounts and it can cause bloating.

**How to use it:** a glass of coconut water plus some salty food (toast with butter, crackers, broth) covers both potassium and sodium. Or add a small pinch of salt to the glass. If you have kidney disease or take medicines that raise potassium levels, such as certain blood pressure drugs or potassium-sparing diuretics, don't drink it in large amounts without checking with your doctor.

For a deeper comparison with sports drinks, see our full guide to [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover).

## Tomato Juice: The Salty Option Most People Overlook

Tomato juice is the closest thing in the juice aisle to a savory rehydration drink. Regular tomato juice and vegetable blends like V8 are high in sodium, and tomatoes also supply potassium, all with much less sugar than fruit juice. If you've been sick or sweated a lot, that salt is actually useful.

That same salt is a downside for some people. A single glass of regular tomato juice can carry a large share of the daily sodium limit many health bodies recommend, so if you have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease, or you're on a low-sodium diet, pick a low-sodium version or skip it. Tomato juice is also acidic, so it can sting if you have heartburn.

**A note on Bloody Marys:** tomato juice's reputation as a hangover drink comes partly from the "hair of the dog" Bloody Mary. Adding vodka to the morning after doesn't treat a hangover. It postpones it while your body processes even more alcohol. Drink the tomato juice plain.

## Orange Juice: Good for Energy, Hard on a Sore Stomach

Orange juice is the juice most people reach for. It gives you fluid, a solid amount of potassium, and fast natural sugar, which can make you feel a bit more human when you've barely eaten. The vitamin C is the part everyone mentions, but it's also the part with the weakest support. There is no good evidence that vitamin C, from juice or from a pill, shortens or eases a hangover in a meaningful way.

The real catch is acidity. Orange juice is acidic, and alcohol has already irritated your stomach lining and increased acid. If you're dealing with heartburn, a burning stomach, or you've been throwing up, orange juice can make you feel worse. In that case, start with water or an electrolyte drink and save the orange juice for later in the day, or dilute it half-and-half with water.

We go into more detail, including how much to drink, in our guide to [orange juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/orange-juice-for-hangover). If heartburn is your main symptom, our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) explains what helps.

## Korean Pear Juice: The Only Juice With a Human Hangover Study

Korean pear juice (also sold as Asian pear juice) is a traditional hangover drink in Korea, and it's the one juice on this list with a bit of hangover-specific research in people. Australian researchers at CSIRO reported a small study in which healthy young men who drank Korean pear juice *before* drinking alcohol reported milder hangovers than those who drank a placebo. When the juice was taken the morning after, it didn't seem to help.

That's interesting, but it's a long way from proof. The study was small, only included young healthy men, and hasn't been widely repeated. It also used juice made from Korean (Asian) pears, not ordinary Western pears.

**How to use it:** if you want to try it, drink a glass shortly before your first drink, not the next morning. Think of it as a low-risk experiment, and don't let it talk you into drinking more than you planned. Our guide to [Korean pear juice for hangovers](/never-hungover/korean-pear-juice-hangover) covers the study and how to choose a product.

## Watermelon Juice: Hydrating and Gentle

Watermelon is about 90% water, so watermelon juice is mostly a pleasant way to get fluid in. It has some potassium and is low in acid, which makes it easier on a sore stomach than citrus. You'll see claims that a compound in watermelon called citrulline "detoxes" the body or speeds up hangover recovery. There is no good evidence for that in people with hangovers.

It's a perfectly fine choice if it sounds good to you, especially chilled. Just remember it has little sodium, so pair it with something salty. Our guide to [watermelon for a hangover](/never-hungover/watermelon-for-hangover) goes through the citrulline claim in detail.

## Pickle Juice: A Salty Shot, Not a Full Drink

Pickle brine isn't a juice in the usual sense, but it's one of the most searched hangover "juices." Its value is simple: it's very salty. A small amount of brine gives you a quick dose of sodium, which helps your body hold on to the water you drink afterward. That can be useful after a night with vomiting or heavy sweating.

Keep the portion small, about 1 to 3 ounces, and follow it with a big glass of water. Skip it if you have high blood pressure, heart or kidney disease, or bad heartburn. Our guide to [pickle juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/pickle-juice-for-hangover) explains how much to drink and who should avoid it.

## Apple, Cranberry, and Grape Juice: Fine, but Mostly Sugar

These three are common in the fridge but don't bring much to a hangover beyond fluid and sugar.

- **Apple juice** is low in acid, which makes it one of the gentlest juices on a queasy stomach. It's also high in sugar with very little potassium or sodium. Diluted half-and-half with water, it's a reasonable way to sip fluids when nothing else appeals.
- **Cranberry juice** is often sold as a "cleansing" drink, but it doesn't flush alcohol out of your body or support your liver in any special way. Most cranberry drinks on shelves are "cocktails" with a lot of added sugar, because pure cranberry juice is very tart.
- **Grape juice** is one of the most sugary juices you can buy. A big glass on an empty stomach can leave you feeling worse once the sugar wears off. If you drink it, keep it small or dilute it.

None of these are harmful in a normal glass. They're just not better than water plus a snack.

## Grapefruit Juice: A Medication Warning

Grapefruit juice deserves its own section because of a well-known safety issue. Grapefruit contains compounds that block an enzyme in your gut (called CYP3A4) that breaks down many medicines. When that enzyme is blocked, more of the drug gets into your blood, sometimes much more. The FDA warns about this for a range of medicines, including some statins (cholesterol drugs), certain blood pressure drugs, some anti-anxiety medicines, and others.

If you take any prescription medicine, check the label or ask a pharmacist before drinking grapefruit juice, hangover or not. It's also quite acidic. For most people, there's no reason to pick it over other juices the morning after.

## Lemon Water and "Detox" Juices

Lemon water is often promoted as a way to "flush toxins" or "cleanse the liver" after drinking. It doesn't do either. Your liver and kidneys clear alcohol and its by-products on their own schedule, and no drink meaningfully speeds that up. Lemon water is still a fine choice for one practical reason: if a squeeze of lemon makes you drink more water, that's helpful.

The same goes for green juices, celery juice, and multi-day "juice cleanses" sold as hangover resets. There is no good evidence that any of them remove alcohol from your body faster or repair your liver. A juice cleanse after a heavy weekend also tends to be low in protein and salt, which are things your body actually needs while it recovers. Regular meals, water, and sleep do more.

## Juice vs. Water vs. Electrolyte Drinks

Juice isn't automatically better than plain water, and it isn't as good as an oral rehydration drink when you're properly dehydrated. Here's how they compare:

- **Plain water** is the foundation. It's free, it has no sugar, and it's what your body needs most. Its weakness is that it has no sodium, so some of it passes straight through if you drink a lot quickly. Our guide on whether [water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) explains why.
- **Oral rehydration drinks** like Pedialyte are designed with a specific balance of sodium, potassium, and sugar that helps your gut absorb water efficiently. They're the best choice after vomiting, diarrhea, or a very heavy night. Sports drinks like Gatorade are a middle ground; see our guide to [Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/gatorade-for-hangover).
- **Juice** sits somewhere in between. It brings potassium and sugar but usually little sodium, so it works best alongside food or a salty snack. Its biggest advantage is that it tastes good, so you're more likely to keep drinking.

If you'd rather make your own, a simple mix of water, a little juice for flavor, and a pinch of salt gets you surprisingly close to a store-bought electrolyte drink. Our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) recipe shows the proportions. For a full plan, see [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## How Much Juice to Drink, and When

A few practical guidelines make juice more helpful and less likely to backfire:

1. **Start with water.** Have a glass of water or an electrolyte drink first, especially if your stomach is unsettled.
2. **Keep the juice portion modest.** About 6 to 8 ounces is plenty. A full liter of juice is a lot of sugar on a stomach that's already struggling.
3. **Dilute if it stings.** Half juice, half water is gentler, still tastes good, and is closer to what your gut absorbs well.
4. **Sip, don't chug.** Drinking quickly when you're nauseous can trigger vomiting. Small sips every few minutes work better.
5. **Eat something.** Toast, crackers, eggs, rice, or a banana alongside your juice helps steady your blood sugar and adds the sodium that most juices lack. See our list of the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).
6. **Go easy if you have diabetes.** Juice raises blood sugar quickly. If you manage diabetes, count juice like any other carbohydrate and keep an eye on your levels, especially since alcohol can also cause low blood sugar.

## What About Juice as a Mixer?

Some people wonder whether mixing alcohol with juice instead of soda makes the next morning easier. The honest answer is that the mixer matters much less than how much alcohol you drink.

A few things are worth knowing. Juice doesn't stop alcohol from being absorbed or broken down, and a sweet, fruity drink can make alcohol harder to taste, which makes it easy to drink more than you meant to. On the other hand, research from Northern Kentucky University found that people who drank vodka with a diet mixer reached higher breath alcohol levels than those who drank it with a regular, sugar-sweetened mixer, likely because the sugar slowed how fast alcohol left the stomach. That doesn't make juice a hangover preventer. It just means "diet" mixers aren't automatically the safer choice.

The biggest levers are still the simple ones: fewer drinks, a slower pace, food in your stomach, and water between drinks. Our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Simple Hangover Juice Combinations

If you want something a little more interesting than a single juice, these combinations play to each ingredient's strengths. None of them are cures, but they're easy on the stomach and help with fluids and electrolytes.

- **Coconut-orange cooler:** half coconut water, half orange juice, over ice. Potassium and sugar from both, with less acid than straight orange juice.
- **Savory tomato sipper:** low-sodium tomato juice with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of black pepper. Sodium and potassium with very little sugar.
- **Gentle ginger-apple:** apple juice diluted with water and a few slices of fresh ginger. Ginger has some evidence for nausea in other settings, though not specifically for hangovers. See our guide to [ginger for a hangover](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover).
- **Watermelon salt-lime:** blended watermelon, a squeeze of lime, and a small pinch of salt. Hydrating, mild, and adds the sodium watermelon lacks.

## Which Juice Should You Pick? A Quick Guide by Symptom

- **Mostly thirsty and tired:** coconut water or diluted orange juice, plus food.
- **Threw up or sweated a lot:** an oral rehydration drink first, then tomato juice or coconut water with a pinch of salt.
- **Nauseous:** small sips of diluted apple juice or watermelon juice, plus plain crackers or toast.
- **Heartburn or burning stomach:** skip orange, tomato, grapefruit, and lemon. Try water, diluted apple juice, or coconut water.
- **Planning ahead for tonight:** Korean pear juice before your first drink, if you want to try it, plus a real meal.
- **Taking prescription medicines:** avoid grapefruit juice unless your pharmacist says it's fine.

## Where DHM Fits In

Juice helps with the fluid and energy side of a hangover, but not with alcohol itself or how your body handles it. Some people add a supplement for that part. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. It also doesn't replace drinking less, eating, or rehydrating.

If you want to try it, it's usually taken with water while drinking or before bed. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

For a closer look at individual juices, see our guides to [apple juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/apple-juice-for-hangover) and [cranberry juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/cranberry-juice-for-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- No juice cures a hangover. The useful ones replace fluid, potassium, and energy, and are gentle on your stomach.
- **Coconut water** and **tomato juice** are the most practical picks. Add salt or salty food to coconut water; choose low-sodium tomato juice if you watch your salt.
- **Orange juice** is fine if your stomach is calm, but its vitamin C does little for a hangover and its acid can worsen heartburn.
- **Korean pear juice** has a small study behind it, but only when taken before drinking.
- Skip "detox" juices and cleanses, go easy on sugary grape and cranberry cocktails, and avoid grapefruit juice if you take prescription medicine.
- If you can't keep fluids down, are vomiting repeatedly, or feel confused or faint, get medical help rather than trying another drink.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best juice for a hangover?**

There's no single best juice, but coconut water and tomato juice are the most practical choices because they replace fluid and electrolytes without a lot of sugar. Coconut water is rich in potassium, and tomato juice adds sodium too. Orange juice is a reasonable option if your stomach feels fine. Whichever you choose, drink water as well and eat something salty, since most juices are low in sodium.

**Is orange juice good for a hangover?**

It can help a little by giving you fluid, potassium, and quick sugar for energy. There is no good evidence that its vitamin C shortens a hangover. Because orange juice is acidic, it can make heartburn or a burning stomach worse, so if your stomach is upset, start with water or an electrolyte drink and dilute the orange juice or save it for later.

**Is juice better than water for a hangover?**

Not necessarily. Water is the foundation of hangover recovery. Juice adds potassium and sugar, which can help if you haven't eaten, but it's usually low in sodium and can be hard on a sore stomach. The best approach for most people is water or an electrolyte drink first, then a modest glass of juice alongside some food.

**Does cranberry juice or lemon water detox your body after drinking?**

No. There is no good evidence that cranberry juice, lemon water, celery juice, or juice cleanses flush alcohol out of your body or help your liver recover faster. Your liver processes alcohol at its own pace. These drinks are fine for hydration if you enjoy them, but they don't have a special detox effect.

**Does Korean pear juice really work for hangovers?**

It's the only juice with a small human study suggesting a benefit. In that study, drinking Korean pear juice before drinking alcohol was linked to milder hangovers, while drinking it the morning after didn't help. The study was small and only included young men, so treat it as a low-risk experiment rather than a reliable fix.

**What juice should I avoid with a hangover?**

Avoid grapefruit juice if you take prescription medicines, because it can change how your body handles many drugs. Go easy on very sugary juices like grape juice and sweetened cranberry cocktails. If you have heartburn, skip acidic juices like orange, tomato, grapefruit, and lemon until your stomach settles. And don't add alcohol to your juice the next morning; a Bloody Mary or mimosa only delays the hangover.

**Can I drink juice if I have diabetes and a hangover?**

Be careful. Juice raises blood sugar quickly, and alcohol can also cause low blood sugar in people taking diabetes medicines, so your levels may swing in either direction the morning after. Count juice like any other carbohydrate, check your blood sugar, and favor water or sugar-free electrolyte drinks. If your numbers are hard to control, talk to your doctor.
